books.section: Topic 7.7 1920s: Innovations in Communication and Technology

primary_sources: Photograph, Frank Conrad's radio station 8XK, July 1920

stimulus.text:
The photograph shows Frank Conrad's radio station 8XK in the garage of his home in Wilkinsburg, Pennsylvania, in July 1920. A wooden table holds coils of wire, glass vacuum tubes, dials, and loose cables.

Background: Conrad's broadcasts led the Westinghouse company to create KDKA in Pittsburgh. KDKA was licensed on October 27, 1920, and on November 2, 1920, it broadcast the returns of the Harding-Cox presidential election.
stimulus.source_note: Photograph, Frank Conrad's radio station 8XK, July 1920, Brown Bros. Photos, public domain (Wikimedia Commons). KDKA facts from the Federal Communications Commission and the Federal Judicial Center.

rationales.A: Election news was the first broadcast, but profit was the motive. Westinghouse wanted to sell radios, not just report news.
rationales.B: KDKA did not replace newspapers. Papers stayed the main news source, and some even ran their own stations.
rationales.C: Background: Westinghouse made radio sets, and a station gave buyers something to listen to. KDKA existed to create demand for the sets it sold.
rationales.D: Westinghouse was a private company. KDKA was a company station, not a government one.
rationales.general:
1. Ask who Westinghouse was: a company that made radio sets.
2. Ask what a set needs: something to listen to, or nobody buys one.
3. Connect the two: a station created the demand that sold the sets.
4. Check the first broadcast: election returns gave listeners a reason to tune in that very night.
Remember: when a maker gives away the content, ask what product the content sells.
